Mill
MIL
noun
From the Old English mylen, from the Late Latin molina, from molere, “to grind”; the household hand-mill of two stones, the upper turned upon the nether to grind grain into meal. The AV millstone names the stone; mill names the whole apparatus and the labour at it.

Biblical Definition

The mill of Scripture is not a building but a pair of stones — the nether stone fixed, the upper turned by hand, usually by two women seated opposite one another, grinding the day’s grain before the day’s bread. It was the lowest and most constant labour of a household, which is why the AV uses it to mark the bottom of a society: the LORD threatens the firstborn of Egypt “from the firstborn of Pharaoh that sitteth upon his throne, even unto the firstborn of the maidservant that is behind the mill” (Exo 11:5). Throne and hand-mill are the two ends of the nation, and judgment reaches both. Israel in the wilderness ground the manna in mills or beat it in a mortar and baked it in pans (Num 11:8) — even bread from heaven was worked by human hands. When Jerusalem fell, the sign of ruin was that “they took the young men to grind” (Lam 5:13), the free man set to the woman’s stone; and blinded Samson turned a Philistine mill in the prison house. The law even fenced the mill about with mercy: no man might take the nether or the upper millstone to pledge, for he taketh a man’s life to pledge (Deu 24:6) — seize a household’s mill and you have seized its bread. Then Christ takes this most ordinary scene and hangs eternity on it: “Two women shall be grinding at the mill; the one shall be taken, and the other left” (Mat 24:41). Two hands on one stone, one destiny apart.

Webster 1828 Definition

An engine or machine for grinding grain; in Scripture, the household hand-mill of two stones.

MILL, a machine for grinding grain and reducing it to meal or flour.

From Old English mylen, Late Latin molina, from molere, “to grind.”

The biblical mill is a hand-mill: a fixed nether stone and a turning upper stone.

The AV millstone names the stone itself; mill names the apparatus and the labour.

Grinding was women’s daily work and, for captives, the badge of servitude (Lam 5:13).

Key Scripture

Exo 11:5 — "And all the firstborn in the land of Egypt shall die, from the firstborn of Pharaoh that sitteth upon his throne, even unto the firstborn of the maidservant that is behind the mill; and all the firstborn of beasts."

Mat 24:41 — "Two women shall be grinding at the mill; the one shall be taken, and the other left."

Num 11:8 — "And the people went about, and gathered it, and ground it in mills, or beat it in a mortar, and baked it in pans, and made cakes of it: and the taste of it was as the taste of fresh oil."

Deu 24:6 — "No man shall take the nether or the upper millstone to pledge: for he taketh a man's life to pledge."

Modern Corruption

Two women at a mill have been conscripted into a secret rapture the passage does not teach.

expand to see more

Mat 24:41 is the standing proof text of dispensational premillennialism — a nineteenth-century novelty of Darby and Scofield unknown to any Reformation confession — which reads the one taken as a believer secretly caught away and the one left as an unbeliever abandoned to a seven-year tribulation. The context will not carry it. The Lord has just compared that day to the days of Noah, when they ate and drank and married until the flood came and took them all away; the taking in the figure He Himself supplies is the taking of judgment, and those left are the preserved. Whichever way the terms are read, the passage teaches one thing plainly and it is not a secret removal: the second coming will be visible as lightning shining from the east unto the west, sudden, and final, and it will fall upon people at their ordinary work with no interval for a second chance.

The doctrine to recover is the ordinariness of the setting and the absoluteness of the separation. Two women sit at one stone, hands on the same handle, grinding the same grain for the same household — nearer to each other than most of us are to anyone — and at that moment the division of eternity passes between them. The last day does not find men in a religious posture; it finds them at the mill, in the field, in the bed. There is no visible difference between the two women that morning, and no one at the mill could have told you which was which; the difference is what God knows and what will then be revealed. That is why Christ closes the passage not with a calendar but with a command: watch therefore, for ye know not what hour your Lord doth come.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

The household hand-mill of two stones — the plainest daily labour, and the scene of the last separation.

expand to see more

Mill — Old English mylen, Latin molere, “to grind.”

A hand-mill of two stones, not a building: nether stone fixed, upper stone turned.

Distinct from millstone, which names the stone itself.

Behind the mill = the bottom of the household (Exo 11:5); to grind = servitude (Lam 5:13).

The law forbade taking a mill in pledge — it is a family’s bread (Deu 24:6).

Usage

"From the throne to the mill: judgment reached both ends of Egypt in one night."

"The mill is the hand-mill of two stones, not a building on a stream."

"Two women grinding at the mill, one taken and one left — the last day finds men at work."
